name: Jules A. Hoffmann
milestone_by_age_26: Published his first scientific paper on aquatic Heteroptera (waterbugs) of Luxembourg at age 17, co-authored with his entomologist father.
early_history_summary: Hoffmann grew up in post-war Luxembourg where his father, a high school biology teacher and amateur entomologist, took him on insect-collecting trips from an early age. By his mid-teens he was identifying species and published his first paper at 17. He went on to study biology at the University of Strasbourg and became a CNRS research assistant by age 23.
family_context_summary: Son of a high school biology teacher in Luxembourg who was a passionate amateur entomologist; father personally guided Hoffmann's early fieldwork and co-authored his first paper.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a biology teacher and systematic entomologist who spent spare time collecting and describing insects, directly transferring domain knowledge and fieldwork skills to his son.
primary_early_advantage_tags: entomologist father, fieldwork mentorship, early publication, Luxembourg, insect biology
evidence_summary: Hoffmann's father was a high school biology teacher and amateur entomologist who took young Jules on collecting trips, leading to a co-authored first paper at 17. This family-domain apprenticeship gave him early entomological expertise and a direct path to biological research. He joined CNRS as a research assistant at 23 and completed his PhD at 28 under Pierre Joly at Strasbourg, studying insect immune defenses. The Nobel Prize for innate immunity discoveries came in 2011, decades after these formative years.
starting_point: Born in Echternach, Luxembourg to a high school biology teacher and amateur entomologist father who guided his early interest in insects.
current_position: Emeritus Research Director at CNRS and professor at University of Strasbourg Institute for Advanced Study; Nobel Laureate in Physiology or Medicine (2011); resides in Strasbourg, France.

trajectory.event: Published his first scientific paper on aquatic Heteroptera of Luxembourg, co-authored with his father.

Awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine jointly with Bruce Beutler for discoveries concerning activation of innate immunity.

name: Tsukasa Hosaka
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Emperor's Cup with Furukawa Electric in 1960 and debuted for the Japan national team in November 1960, becoming a regular goalkeeper for Japan in the early 1960s.
early_history_summary: Hosaka was born in Kofu, Yamanashi, and played youth football at Kofu Daiichi High School before attending Meiji University from 1955 to 1958. He joined Furukawa Electric in 1959 and quickly became their goalkeeper, winning the Emperor's Cup in his first year. He was selected for the Japan national team in 1960 and became a regular in the early 1960s.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Meiji University, Furukawa Electric, Emperor's Cup, Japan national team, company club
evidence_summary: Hosaka played at Meiji University, one of Japan's prominent football programs, before joining Furukawa Electric's company-backed club in 1959. He won the Emperor's Cup in 1960 and 1961 and debuted for Japan in November 1960, becoming a regular goalkeeper through the early 1960s including the 1962 Asian Games and 1964 Olympics selection. Family background is not documented in reviewed sources. His career reflected Japan's postwar company-club football system.
starting_point: Born in Kofu, Yamanashi, Japan; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Died in January 2018 at age 80 in Kofu, Yamanashi, Japan; final role: manager of Kofu SC (1973-1977) after retirement as a player.

name: Toru Takemitsu
milestone_by_age_26: Made his public debut as a composer in December 1950 at age 20 with the piano piece 'Lento in Due Movimenti' performed at the 7th New Composers Association Concert at Yomiuri Hall, Tokyo.
early_history_summary: Takemitsu was born in Tokyo and moved to Japanese-controlled Dalian as an infant, where his father was a government official. After his father's death in 1938, he returned to Japan. Largely self-taught, he discovered Western classical music during wartime military service and later through U.S. Armed Forces radio broadcasts while hospitalized with tuberculosis. He studied briefly under Yasuji Kiyose and assisted Fumio Hayasaka with film music before his 1950 debut.
family_context_summary: Son of a Japanese government official stationed in Dalian, Manchuria; father died in 1938 when Takemitsu was 8, leaving the family in reduced circumstances. He was sent back to Japan to live with an aunt and uncle.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a government official with a passion for jazz records and shakuhachi, exposing Takemitsu to music early, though the father died when Toru was young and had limited direct influence on his compositional training.
primary_early_advantage_tags: self-taught, Kiyose mentorship, Hayasaka film music, postwar Japan, avant-garde
evidence_summary: Takemitsu was largely self-taught, discovering Western music through military service and U.S. occupation radio. He studied briefly under Yasuji Kiyose and assisted Fumio Hayasaka with film music, gaining practical compositional experience. His father's early death and wartime displacement created hardship but also exposure to diverse musical influences. He debuted at 20 and co-founded the avant-garde Jikken Kōbō group at 21, positioning himself at Japan's postwar artistic frontier. His breakthrough came when Stravinsky praised his Requiem for Strings in 1959.
starting_point: Born in Tokyo to a government official father stationed in Dalian, Manchuria; father died when Takemitsu was 8, leaving the family in modest circumstances in postwar Japan.
current_position: Died on February 20, 1996 at age 65 in Tokyo; final role: internationally renowned composer and professor who composed hundreds of works and scored over 90 films.

trajectory.event: Made his public debut as a composer with 'Lento in Due Movimenti' performed at the 7th New Composers Association Concert at Yomiuri Hall, Tokyo.

Composed the film score for Akira Kurosawa's 'Dodes'ka-den', establishing himself as a leading film composer.
Died on February 20, 1996 in Tokyo, leaving a legacy of hundreds of compositions and over 90 film scores.

name: Ngô Bảo Châu
milestone_by_age_26: Won a gold medal with a perfect score (42/42) at the 1988 International Mathematical Olympiad at age 15, and a second gold medal in 1989, becoming the first Vietnamese student to win two IMO gold medals.
early_history_summary: Châu was born in Hanoi to an intellectual family: his father was a professor of physics and his mother a physician. His father, returning from a doctoral degree in the Soviet Union, enrolled Châu in special mathematics classes for gifted students. At age 15, Châu entered the specialized mathematics class at the High School for Gifted Students, Hanoi University of Science, and immediately competed at the IMO, achieving a perfect score.
family_context_summary: Born into an intellectual family in Hanoi; father was a professor of physics at the Vietnam National Institute of Mechanics who had earned his PhD in the Soviet Union, and mother was a physician and associate professor at a traditional medicine hospital.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a professor of applied mathematics/physics who actively directed Châu's early mathematical education, enrolling him in gifted-student programs and providing mathematical exercises from a young age.
primary_early_advantage_tags: professor father, gifted school, IMO gold, perfect score, Hanoi, mathematical prodigy
evidence_summary: Châu's father, a physics professor who had studied in the Soviet Union, actively cultivated his son's mathematical talent by enrolling him in Vietnam's specialized gifted-student track. At 15, Châu won a perfect-score gold medal at the 1988 IMO and repeated with another gold in 1989, becoming the first Vietnamese to win two IMO golds. He then studied at École Normale Supérieure in Paris and earned his PhD from Université Paris-Sud in 1997. He was awarded the Fields Medal in 2010 for proving the Fundamental Lemma in the Langlands program.
starting_point: Born in Hanoi, Vietnam to a professor of physics father (who earned a PhD in the Soviet Union) and a physician mother, both university-level academics.
current_position: Professor of mathematics at the University of Chicago and scientific director of the Vietnam Institute for Advanced Study in Mathematics; Fields Medal recipient (2010); moving to HKU.

trajectory.event: Won a gold medal with a perfect score (42/42) at the International Mathematical Olympiad in Australia.

Awarded the Fields Medal at the International Congress of Mathematicians in Hyderabad for his proof of the Fundamental Lemma.

name: Peter Grünberg
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Grünberg completed his diploma thesis at age 26 (1965-1966) and his PhD at 29 (1969), both standard academic steps. His Nobel Prize-winning discovery of giant magnetoresistance came in 1988 at age 49.
early_history_summary: Grünberg was born in Pilsen (now Czech Republic) to a Sudeten German family; his father, a mechanical engineer, died in the last days of WWII. The family was resettled to Lauterbach in Hesse, Germany, in 1946. He studied physics at the University of Frankfurt from 1959 and continued at Darmstadt Technical University, completing his diploma in 1966 and PhD in 1969.
family_context_summary: Born to a Sudeten German family in Pilsen; father was a mechanical engineer (Dipl.-Ing.) who worked for Skoda designing locomotives and died during the last days of WWII; mother raised two children alone after resettlement to West Germany.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father held a diploma in mechanical engineering from the Technical University of Bruenn and worked at Skoda factory in Pilsen, but died when Grünberg was young, limiting direct domain transfer.
evidence_summary: Grünberg's father was a mechanical engineer who died during WWII, leaving his mother to raise two children alone in postwar West Germany. He studied physics at Frankfurt and Darmstadt, completing his diploma at 26 and PhD at 29 — standard academic progression without a notable early milestone. His Nobel Prize-winning discovery of giant magnetoresistance (GMR) came in 1988 at age 49, well after age 26.

name: Andrei Tarkovsky
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Tarkovsky's student films at VGIK (The Killers, 1956; There Will Be No Leave Today, 1959) were academic exercises. His first feature film, Ivan's Childhood, which won the Golden Lion at Venice, was released in 1962 when he was 30.
early_history_summary: Tarkovsky was born in Zavrzhe (now Belarus) to poet Arseni Tarkovsky and actress Maria Ivanovna Vishnyakova. His parents divorced when he was young. He studied Arabic at the Moscow Institute of Oriental Languages (1951-1954), then worked on a geological expedition in Siberia before enrolling at VGIK film school in 1954 under Mikhail Romm. He made student films during his time at VGIK but his breakthrough came with his diploma film and first feature after age 26.
family_context_summary: Son of noted poet Arseni Tarkovsky and actress Maria Ivanovna Vishnyakova; parents divorced when he was young, and his father left the family, creating financial hardship.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a prominent poet and mother a literary corrector/actress, providing a culturally rich but financially strained upbringing in the Soviet artistic milieu.
evidence_summary: Tarkovsky was the son of poet Arseni Tarkovsky and grew up in a culturally rich but financially strained Soviet household after his parents divorced. He studied Arabic and geology before enrolling at VGIK at age 22. His student films (The Killers, 1956; There Will Be No Leave Today, 1959) were collaborative academic exercises, not material career milestones. His diploma film The Steamroller and the Violin was completed in 1960 at age 28, and his first feature Ivan's Childhood won the Golden Lion at Venice in 1962 at age 30 — both after age 26.

name: Francisco Ibáñez Talavera
milestone_by_age_26: Created and published the first Mortadelo y Filemón comic strip on January 20, 1958, at age 21, in the magazine Pulgarcito — a series that became one of the most iconic in Spanish comics history.
early_history_summary: Ibáñez was born in Barcelona to a lower-middle-class family; his father was an accountant from Alicante and his mother was from Andalusia. He showed drawing talent from childhood and published his first drawing at age 11 in the magazine Chicos. From 1950 to 1957 he worked at a bank while simultaneously creating comic series for various magazines, and in 1957 he committed to comics full-time, joining Editorial Bruguera where he created Mortadelo y Filemón in 1958.
family_context_summary: Born in a working-class neighborhood of Barcelona to a lower-middle-class family; father was an accountant from Alicante and mother was a homemaker from Andalusia; had three siblings.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was an accountant, not directly connected to comics or art, but supported young Francisco's drawing interests; no documented domain transfer in artistic fields.

evidence_summary: Ibáñez grew up in a modest Barcelona household with no artistic family background but showed drawing talent from childhood, publishing his first drawing at 11. From ages 14-21 he simultaneously worked at a bank and created comic series for multiple magazines, building extensive early reps. In 1957 he committed to comics full-time and joined Editorial Bruguera, where he created Mortadelo y Filemón in January 1958 at age 21 — a series that became a cultural icon of Spanish comics. His early immersion in Barcelona's comic publishing ecosystem and prolific output were key advantages.
starting_point: Born in a working-class neighborhood of Barcelona, Spain to a lower-middle-class family; father was an accountant and mother a homemaker.

name: Oscar Panno
milestone_by_age_26: Won the World Junior Chess Championship in 1953 at age 18 and the Argentine national championship the same year; became a grandmaster at 20 in 1955 and placed third at the Gothenburg Interzonal, qualifying for the Candidates Tournament.
early_history_summary: Panno was born in Buenos Aires and learned chess from his father at age 6. He joined the Club Atlético River Plate chess room at 12 and became 'chess addicted.' His competitive career began in 1951, and in 1953 he won both the World Junior Championship in Copenhagen and the Argentine national championship. He became a grandmaster at 20 and placed third at the 1955 Interzonal, qualifying for the Candidates Tournament.
family_context_summary: Born in Buenos Aires; father taught him chess at age 6 and played with him and his older brother on rainy days; grandfather had a library with chess textbooks by Bogoljubow that advanced his early learning.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a chess enthusiast who taught Panno the rules at age 6 and provided a chess-playing environment at home; grandfather's library contained chess textbooks that furthered his self-education.

He joined Club Atlético River Plate's chess room at 12, immersing himself in Buenos Aires's strong chess culture shaped by pre-war European émigrés like Najdorf. At 18 he won the World Junior Championship and Argentine national title; at 20 he became a grandmaster and placed third at the Gothenburg Interzonal, qualifying for the Candidates Tournament. He later stepped back from professional chess to study civil engineering (1958-1962) but remained a competitive player for decades.

name: Edwin van der Sar
milestone_by_age_26: Won the UEFA Champions League with Ajax in May 1995 at age 24, having already won multiple Eredivisie titles and the Dutch Cup as Ajax's first-choice goalkeeper.
early_history_summary: Van der Sar was born in Voorhout, Netherlands, and played youth football at Foreholte (1980-1985) and Noordwijk (1985-1990). He joined Ajax at a relatively late age in 1990 and debuted for the first team on April 23, 1991, at age 20. After serving as reserve keeper behind Stanley Menzo, he became Ajax's #1 goalkeeper in 1993 and won the Dutch Cup that year, followed by Eredivisie titles and the Champions League in 1995.
family_context_summary: Born in Voorhout, a village in the Dutch countryside; family background not extensively documented beyond his parents Rien and Willie van der Sar.

He debuted in April 1991 and became first-choice keeper in 1993 after Menzo's errors. By 26 he had won the Dutch Cup (1993), two Eredivisie titles (1994, 1995), and the Champions League (1995). His height (1.98m) and ball-playing ability suited the sweeper-keeper role. Family background is not well documented in reviewed sources.

name: Egon Franke
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Polish junior championship in foil in 1955 at age 19, followed by the senior vice-championship in 1957 and national team selection, culminating in Olympic participation at the 1960 Rome Games at age 24.
early_history_summary: Franke was born in Gleiwitz (now Gliwice, Poland) to a gasworks employee father. He began fencing at Budowlanych Gliwice in 1952, trained by Antoni Franz. He moved to Legia Warszawa during military service (1955-1957) under coach Andrzej Przeździecki, then returned to Piast Gliwice. He won the Polish junior foil championship in 1955, senior vice-championship in 1957, and joined the national team that same year.
family_context_summary: Born in Gleiwitz (now Gliwice, Poland) to Franz Franke, a gasworks employee, and Elfriede Tschentschel; worked as a technical draftsman at a steelworks before his fencing career took off.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a gasworks employee; no documented connection to fencing or sports in the family background.

evidence_summary: Franke grew up in a working-class family in Gliwice, Poland, with his father employed at the local gasworks. He began fencing at 17 under coach Antoni Franz at Budowlanych Gliwice, then trained under Andrzej Przeździecki at Legia Warszawa during military service. He won the Polish junior foil championship at 19 (1955), senior vice-championship at 21 (1957), and joined the national team under coach Zbigniew Czajkowski. Despite injuries (eye, lung, chronic illness), his technical classical style and dedicated coaching led to Olympic gold in 1964. His wife Elżbieta Franke-Cymerman was also an Olympic fencer.
starting_point: Born in Gleiwitz (now Gliwice, Poland) to a gasworks employee father and mother Elfriede Tschentschel; working-class family in postwar Silesia.
current_position: Died on March 30, 2022 at age 86 in Chieri, Turin, Italy; final role: fencing coach in Italy, where he lived with his wife Elżbieta Franke-Cymerman, also an Olympic fencer.
